name: Shortgrass prairie
notes: Sod-forming grasses under 0.5 m (blue grama, buffalograss) with scattered yucca, cactus and low sage on the dry western Great Plains (Colorado, Wyoming, Texas panhandle); treeless except along draws.

canopy.name: Plains cottonwood
canopy.source: Populus deltoides ssp. monilifera, N American plains along streams, 15-30 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: massive trunk forking high into a broad crown

growth.juvenile_note: Cottony seed germinates within 24-48 h on wet, bare sandbars and mud flats; the seedling has two minute cotyledons and grows slowly for about 3 weeks, then very fast. Dense, even-aged thickets of slender single-stemmed whips form along river bars, with large triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that flutter; saplings add 1.5-3.5 m a year on good sites.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (P. deltoides: germination within 48 h; slow first 3 weeks then very rapid; seed from 5-10 yr, plains ~10 yr; 1.8-3.7 m/yr; very intolerant of shade; short-lived, 80-90 yr); USDA FEIS (eastern 100-200 yr, plains ~90 yr; 3-58 m tall).

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics vol. 2 (flowers Feb-Apr east, Apr-May plains, before leaves; male catkins 8-13 cm, female 15-30 cm; 3-4-valved capsules with 30-60 seeds ripen in 30-60 days; up to 48 million seeds per tree; wind pollinated); FEIS (capsules 0.8-1.5 cm). Colour is the red male catkins.

canopy.name: Honey mesquite
canopy.origin: SW United States and northern Mexico
canopy.source: Prosopis glandulosa, Tamaulipan thornscrub/Chihuahuan Desert (Mexico, SW USA), thorny deciduous legume 5-12 m — Wikipedia / USDA Plants

traits.native_range: Prosopis glandulosa, Tamaulipan thornscrub/Chihuahuan Desert (Mexico, SW USA), thorny deciduous legume 5-12 m — Wikipedi

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: low wide feathery crown on crooked trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two thick oblong cotyledons, a first once-pinnate leaf, then bright green, feathery bipinnate leaves with a few pairs of long leaflets and paired spines at the nodes of a zigzag stem. The taproot races ahead and a bud zone at the stem base resprouts if the top is killed, so young plants become low, thorny, multi-stemmed bushes; suppressed plants decades old can look like seedlings.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Prosopis glandulosa (scarified seed germinates in ~7 h at 33 C; best emergence from 0.5-1.5 cm; seed by age 3; 27-yr-old plants 0.2-1.5 m in an exclosure; trees 6-12 m; max ages 110-217 yr, most under 100); ICRAF Agroforestree (3-9 m; first fruit at 3-4 yr).

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS P. glandulosa (spring racemes with the leaves; bee pollinated, 160+ bee species; pods 10-20 cm, ~12 seeds, mature in 2-3 months, fall by late summer; 97-131 pods/tree in one study); ICRAF (racemes 5-14 cm; pods 8-30 cm, straw-yellow or violet-tinged). Flowers per raceme, fruit set and decay estimated.

canopy.name: Netleaf hackberry
canopy.source: Celtis reticulata, canyon bottoms and rocky slopes, SW USA and N Mexico, 5-12 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.trunk: short twisted trunk, heavy low limbs, wind-shaped
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.note: thick rough leaves, prominently net-veined beneath

canopy.silhouette: gnarled small tree, warty grey bark, irregular crown

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two notched, rounded cotyledons, then small rough leathery ovate leaves with a lopsided base and a raised net of veins below. The seedling is a thin zig-zag whip that grows slowly; drought, browsing and resprouting often make it a crooked, several-stemmed small tree.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Celtis laevigata var. reticulata (grows slowly, usually 2-6 m, to 16 m; lives 100-200 yr; flowers Apr-May with the leaves; drupes orange-red to purple or black, sweet, persist through winter; abundant crops most years; 120-day cold stratification, 37-80% germination)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Celtis laevigata var. reticulata (inconspicuous flowers with the new leaves Apr-May; drupe ~6 mm stone, orange-red to purple, sweet pulp eaten by birds, mammals and people; ripens late summer-fall and persists into winter; heavy crops nearly every year)

canopy.name: Pinchot juniper
canopy.origin: Southern Great Plains, Texas to New Mexico
canopy.source: Juniperus pinchotii, redberry juniper of the Rolling Plains, Texas panhandle breaks, western Oklahoma and SE New Mexico: a bushy many-stemmed juniper 2-6 m with copper-red berries that, unlike most junipers, resprouts from the base after fire — USDA FEIS / Flora of North America

leaf.note: yellow-green scale leaves in pairs or threes, each with a resin gland; needle-like juvenile leaves

canopy.silhouette: bushy yellow-green juniper, several stems from the ground

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings start with soft, sharp juvenile needles and grow slowly into a prickly little bush, usually under the shade of a mesquite or another shrub. Scale leaves take over within a few years. Top-killed by fire or cutting, it sprouts again from buds at the base, so old plants are dense clumps of several crooked stems rather than single trees.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Juniperus pinchotii (shrub or small tree to ~6 m; sprouts from basal buds after top-kill, unlike Ashe and Utah juniper; slow-growing; seedlings establish under nurse plants). Ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America Juniperus pinchotii (dioecious; seed cones 6-8 mm, copper-red to red, glaucous, maturing in one year; autumn pollen season reported from Texas aerobiology). Timings and crop estimated.

bark.notes: grey-brown bark shredding in thin fibrous strips on several crooked stems

leaf.notes: yellow-green scale leaves, each with a small glandular pit oozing resin

flower.form: tiny tan pollen cones at the tips of male plants

fruit.form: copper-red berry-like cones 6-8 mm on female plants

appearance.silhouette: bushy yellow-green juniper clumps scattered on red breaks above shortgrass
appearance.refs: USDA FEIS; Flora of North America vol. 2

shrub.name: Fringed sage
shrub.origin: N American plains and Eurasian steppe
shrub.source: Artemisia frigida, N American plains and Eurasian steppe, silver sub-shrub 0.2-0.5 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Artemisia frigida, N American plains and Eurasian steppe, silver sub-shrub 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two tiny cotyledons, then finely cut, silky silver leaves forming a small silvery rosette; seed must lie on or near the surface to come up. It becomes a low, mat-like cushion 15-30 cm wide of soft, feathery, silver-grey foliage on a woody base, the stems often rooting where they touch the ground; in late summer many slender stems carry small nodding yellow button heads.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Artemisia frigida: mean germination 5.3-5.4 d; emergence 69% from 2.5 mm, none from 7.5 mm; 3-yr establishment before flowering on dryland; plants 10-35 cm tall, 15-30 cm wide, taproot to 1.6 m; tolerates moderate shade; 38% resprout after fire, recovery in ~3 yr. Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Artemisia frigida: heads of 10-17 ray and 25-50 disc florets; buds early Aug, full bloom ~2 wk later, seed ripe by mid-Sep (mixed-grass prairie); ~3.9 million seeds/lb; wind-dispersed ~1.4 m; under half of plants seed in good years, none in dry. Pollination guild, fruit set and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Plains prickly pear

shrub.silhouette: low clump of spiny flat pads

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two fleshy cotyledons, then a tiny round stem that flattens into a first small pad covered in long, slender spines. It stays low, adding small, flat, very spiny pads that lie on or near the ground and shrivel in drought and winter cold, slowly forming mats up to 2-3 m wide; pads that break off root into new plants.
growth.source: Wikipedia Opuntia polyacantha (10-30 cm tall, mats 2-3 m wide; pads to 27 x 18 cm; very variable spines; flowers yellow, magenta or red; fruit cylindrical, brown, dry and spiny, edible once skin and seeds removed; prairie, sagebrush, pine woodland); ages and establishment rates estimated (USDA FEIS notes slow growth)

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (flowers with tepals 2.5-4 cm, yellow, magenta or red, fading pink-orange; fruit cylindrical, brownish, dry and spiny, eaten raw or as candy once skin and seeds are removed); early-summer flowering, bees (Diadasia, Lithurgus) and beetles as in other plains Opuntia; timings and crop estimated

shrub.name: Rubber rabbitbrush
shrub.source: Ericameria nauseosa, western N America, 0.6-2 m shrub with yellow autumn flowers — USDA PLANTS

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: grey-green rounded shrub, gold flower top

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two small oval cotyledons, then thread-like grey-green leaves on white-felted stems while the root races down. By year 2 it is a small rounded bush of many erect, flexible, whitish-woolly green stems from the base, already topped with yellow flower clusters; full grown in about 4 years. Resprouts from stem buds after fire.
growth.source: USDA FEIS species review (Ericameria nauseosa): germination 5-20 days without stratification (T50 5-96 days by seed source); plants 'full grown' within 4 years (Stanton); post-fire epicormic sprouting. Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (flowering Jul-Oct by elevation; seed ripe late Sep-Nov; plumed achenes wind-dispersed up to ~150 m; good crops every 1-2 yr, fruit fill variable; no persistent seed bank). Head size, heads per cluster, crop and rot estimated.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two narrow, woolly cotyledons, then narrow grey-green leaves thick with white star-shaped hairs. Seeds germinate even in near-freezing soil in early spring; the young plant is a small, woolly, silver-grey sprig with a deep taproot, branching from the base into a low, twiggy subshrub that turns white with fluffy fruits by autumn.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Krascheninnikovia lanata, the North American winterfat: 20-80 cm, flowers Jun-Aug, wind-pollinated, hairy-bracted fruits dispersed fall-winter, may seed in the first year, germinates at near-freezing temperatures). Eurasian K. ceratoides is taller. Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA WPSM (small grey-green wind-pollinated flowers Jun-Aug; one-seeded fruit in two bracts with tufts of white hairs 2-8 mm; disperses fall-winter; abundant annual crops). Timings, set and counts estimated.

shrub.name: Broom snakeweed

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need no chilling and come up after spring or summer rain. The seedling is a single green stem with thread-narrow, resin-dotted leaves; it branches from the base in its first season and by the second is a small, rounded broom of many slender green stems, woody only at the base, topped in late summer with a flat spray of tiny yellow heads.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Gutierrezia sarothrae (subshrub 10-90 cm; short-lived, most plants under 10 yr, some to 20; seedlings flower in the first or second year; flowers Aug-Oct; populations cycle with wet years).

shrub.source: Gutierrezia sarothrae (Pursh) Britton & Rusby, broom snakeweed: rounded resinous subshrub 0.1-0.9 m of overgrazed and eroded plains, benches and badland slopes from the Dakotas and Montana to Mexico. Kew POWO; USDA FEIS; Flora of North America.

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout within days after a good rain, but the seedling lives only if a second wet spell lets it grow adventitious roots about two weeks after emergence. It is a tiny tuft of fine, curly, blue-green leaves that tillers into a dense low bunch or sod and can flower within two months, raising one-sided 'eyelash' seed heads.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Bouteloua gracilis (adventitious roots ~14 d after emergence, seedlings can flower at 2 months, not shade tolerant, 15-30 cm, flowers Jul-Aug to Oct); germination speed and plant longevity from shortgrass-steppe studies (Lauenroth, Coffin), approximate.

growth.juvenile_note: Hard burs hold several seeds that sprout slowly over weeks. The seedling is a tiny tuft of fine, curly, grey-green leaves that soon sends wiry stolons creeping over bare ground, rooting at the nodes into a low, dense, curly turf; male plants raise little flag-like spikes above the leaves, females hide bur clusters among them.
growth.source: Wikipedia (dioecious, 1-30 cm, stolons extend 15-45 cm per season, burs 3-4 mm with 3-7 spikelets, germination low without scarification but prolonged); size and lifespan timings estimated. lifespan_years is the rooted stolon plant; clones persist indefinitely.

Bunches enlarge by new crown tillers (each tiller lives about two seasons) into a fine, fountain-like tussock that sends up spikes of long, curly-awned 'needle and thread' seeds in early summer.
growth.source: NDSU autecology of needle and thread (tillers live two growing seasons, regeneration mainly by crown tillers, low seedling success, flowers late May-June); USDA NRCS Plant Guide (seed dormancy, slow establishment, flowers June, seed July); germination, growth and lifespan values estimated.

ground.name: Great hairy screw-moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores or broken leaves sprout into a green thread-web on bare soil and quickly bud upright shoots. Shoots grow a few millimetres a season, only while wet, building loose yellow-green tufts and patches between grass clumps; dry for most of the year, the patch looks brown-black and crisp, then turns green within a minute of rain.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 27 (shoots 1-4 cm, leaves with recurved margins and a long white awn, twisted when dry, squarrose when moist; on soil, rock and bark from desert to arctic); Oliver et al. on desiccation tolerance. Growth and ages estimated from moss biology.
